solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: The wine that could be poisoned in a P D James mystery

definitions.text: The wine that could be poisoned
definitions.meaning: first meaning: Black Tower is a well-known brand of German white wine, so a bottle of it could be spiked
second meaning: a 1975 Adam Dalgliesh detective novel by P D James

explanation.surface: A detective-story reader wonders which bottle in the plot carries the poison.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a question about a murder method, but it simply names a German wine brand that shares its name with the novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title and the wine's trade name are identical, so one phrase satisfies both halves of the clue.

clue.text: Barnes's love triangle kit? — without the French involved

definitions.text: Barnes's love triangle kit? — without the French involved

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and intricate, so the remaining letters are rearranged
to be without something is to lack it, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
le is the French masculine word for 'the'; it comes off the end of the middle word

explanation.surface: A wry suggestion that Julian Barnes's novel is a do-it-yourself love triangle, minus the French bits.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove LE from TRIANGLE and shuffle the rest of LOVE TRIANG KIT into TALKING IT OVER. Read whole, the clue describes the book: Barnes's 1991 novel of two friends and the woman between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Julian Barnes's novel tells its love triangle through the three characters addressing the reader in turn.

clue.text: British writer of plays, who specialised in comedy

definitions.text: British writer of plays, who specialised in comedy

parts.note: surface reading: a British dramatist known for comedies
setter's reading: a comedian whose running joke was boasting about 'the plays what I wrote'

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a search for a playwright such as Ayckbourn. In the Morecambe and Wise shows the shorter half of the double act claimed to have written the sketches, guest stars and all.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedian's catchphrase about 'the plays what I wrote' made him a fictional playwright, while comedy was his real trade.

clue.text: I call a revolutionary "secular"

indicators.note: a revolution overturns the existing order, so the letters are turned into a new sequence

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone describes a radical as having no religious allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like the noun being labelled, but it is the signal to rearrange the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Laical relates to the laity, people outside the clergy, so it means non-religious or worldly.

clue.text: Culture regularly provides a bit of information

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Cultural life routinely supplies a nugget of knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer describes itself: the crossword solver gets exactly this from every line of the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue is a hint or piece of evidence pointing toward a solution, a small fragment of knowledge.

clue.text: Cronin's top title, one he'd contrived

definitions.text: Cronin's top title, one he'd contrived

indicators.note: contrived means artificially put together, so the letters are made into a new arrangement
the top of a word in a down clue is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter
taken as written
a means one
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A note on which of A J Cronin's invented stories is his best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top title' reads as 'best book', but 'top' takes only the first letter of 'Cronin's'. Read whole, the clue still describes his most famous novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Cronin's 1937 novel about a doctor's career was his biggest success, so it is fairly his top title.

clue.text: Achieve something with humour, holding a particular view

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: wit is clever humour
an angle is a point of view on a subject

explanation.surface: Getting your way by joking while sticking to an opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With humour' reads as manner, but it supplies the outer word; 'with' belongs to the fragment, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To wangle something is to obtain it by cunning or persuasion, so the phrase means managing to get a result.

clue.text: Sailor trapped by traitor in an Atlantic port

indicators.note: something trapped is shut inside its captor, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a rat is someone who betrays their side
AB, able-bodied seaman, is the standard crossword sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman is caught by a turncoat in a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like part of the trap, but it only links the wordplay to the place.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Morocco stands on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Bou Regreg river.

clue.text: A timely prize-winning title?

parts.note: surface reading: a book that won an award at just the right moment
setter's reading: John Harrison won the government's prize by solving a navigation problem with a clock, as told in Dava Sobel's book

explanation.walkthrough: Fixing a ship's east-west position needed accurate time at sea; Harrison's chronometers earned the reward, and Sobel's 1995 bestseller tells the story.
explanation.definitionFit: Dava Sobel's book is about the 18th-century prize for measuring position at sea by timekeeping.

clue.text: Point outside of India that has some pyramids

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for a place: somewhere that has pyramids

parts.note: the nub is the central point of a matter

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its outer edge, so only its two end letters are used

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A geography note about a place beyond India that has pyramids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'India' looks like a whole place or the NATO letter I, but only its outer letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient region along the Nile in modern Sudan holds more pyramids than Egypt, built by Kushite kings.

clue.text: Kentish gentleman and revolutionary a northern leader nixed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over completely, so all the letters are rearranged
a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Kent squire and a rebel get rid of a northern chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' looks like the northern chief, but it does two jobs: it picks the first letter of 'northern' and its own letters join the fodder. Fitting, as Iden killed the rebel Jack Cade.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 2 this squire of Kent kills the rebel Jack Cade in his garden and is knighted.

clue.text: One who came, to kill in cold blood?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the title figure of Eugene O'Neill's play whose name ends 'Cometh', the archaic form of 'comes'

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the person who does it: a cold-blooded killer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: slang for a contract killer, from 'ice' meaning to murder

explanation.surface: A visitor arrives with murderous intent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came' is the plain past of O'Neill's archaic 'cometh'; the question mark flags the loose fit of the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Neill's play awaits a deliveryman who brings ice, and in underworld slang the same word names a hired assassin.

clue.text: British novelist's intrusion that's about to …

parts.note: in geology a sill is a sheet of igneous rock intruded between layers

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the next

parts.note: i.e., id est, means 'that is'
taken as written

explanation.surface: The ellipsis runs into the next clue, as if a writer's interruption is about to capture something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' looks like a phrase meaning 'on the point of', but 'about' wraps the separate word 'to'. 'Intrusion' is a geology term, not a social one.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Sillitoe was the English author of Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, a leading working-class novelist.

clue.text: Caine's key position in British film-making?

definitions.text: Caine's key position in British film-making?

parts.words: Caine's key position in British film-making
parts.note: surface reading: Michael Caine's leading role in British cinema
setter's reading: the actor playing 007 holds the starring job in the long-running spy franchise; Hall Caine wrote a novel of this title

explanation.walkthrough: The Caine is not Michael but the Manx novelist Hall Caine, whose 1890 novel shares its title with a jokey label for whoever plays James Bond.
explanation.definitionFit: Hall Caine's novel title, read as two words, describes the star of the Bond films, a prized casting in British cinema.

clue.text: … capture one in spirit

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

parts.note: gin is a spirit
a means one

explanation.surface: Continued from the previous clue: an attempt to bottle something in alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots join this to the clue before; 'spirit' suggests a ghost or mood, but it is the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To capture and to gain both mean to win or take possession of something.

clue.text: Rocky lairs I have, as a mythical mother

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady and shaken about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A legendary mother boasts of owning stony dens, like the wolf's cave of Roman myth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' reads as describing the lairs, but it is the instruction to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman legend this Vestal Virgin bore the twins Romulus and Remus to the god Mars.

clue.text: Speed worked for this gentleman

parts.note: surface reading: someone whose quickness served him well
setter's reading: Speed is the clownish servant in Shakespeare's The Two Gentlemen of Verona

explanation.walkthrough: 'Speed' is a name, not velocity; 'gentleman' hints at the play's title, where Speed waits on one of the two gentlemen.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Two Gentlemen of Verona the servant Speed is employed by one of the title pair, Proteus's friend.

clue.text: An Irish sea island once had Charlie and a prince as men living in cells

definitions.note: adjectival: like or relating to monks

parts.note: Mona is the old Latin name for the Isle of Man (also used of Anglesey)
C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet
Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V

explanation.surface: A history note about an island that once held a prince and his friend as prisoners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cells' suggests a jail, but these are monks' cells; 'Irish sea' is really the Irish Sea, where the island lies.
explanation.definitionFit: Monachal means monastic, describing the life of monks who sleep and pray in individual small rooms.

clue.text: The last character in Pickwick Papers?

definitions.text: The last character in Pickwick Papers?

parts.words: The last character in Pickwick Papers
parts.note: surface reading: the final person to appear in Dickens's novel
setter's reading: a last is the foot-shaped mould on which shoes are made, so this character works with one; Dickens has one in the Fleet prison

explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' means not final but a shoemaker's mould; Mr Pickwick shares a room in the Fleet debtors' prison with such a tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe-mender works over a last, and Pickwick's Fleet roommate is a mender of shoes imprisoned for debt.

clue.text: Where you'll see Lee at first in depressed part of Gloucestershire

indicators.note: in puts one thing inside another

parts.note: sad means low in spirits

indicators.note: at first means at the beginning, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A guide to the low-lying valley where you can spot the writer Laurie Lee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed' sounds like low-lying ground, and fits the steep valley, but it supplies a word for unhappy.
explanation.definitionFit: This Cotswold valley village near Stroud was Laurie Lee's childhood home, the setting of Cider with Rosie.

clue.text: Online confusion — a source of trouble in South America?

definitions.text: a source of trouble in South America?

indicators.note: confusion is disorder, so the letters come out of sequence

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Internet chaos is blamed as a cause of problems in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by description: the weather pattern is first noticed off Peru and Ecuador.
explanation.definitionFit: This periodic warming of the eastern Pacific brings floods and ruined fisheries to the Pacific coast of the continent.

clue.text: Very short bit of verse about a poet

indicators.note: something short falls short of its full length, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: the word without its last letter

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a line is a single row of a poem
taken as written

explanation.surface: A very brief fragment of poetry concerning a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very short' reads as an intensifier for brevity, but 'Very' is the word to clip.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Verlaine was a French Symbolist poet, author of Romances sans paroles and companion of Rimbaud.

clue.text: Rhymester engaged in Japanese poetry? Just the reverse

indicators.note: it swaps the roles in the clue, so the poetry is what sits within the earlier words rather than the other way round

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A versifier gets caught up in writing Japanese poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, a rhymester is engaged in Japanese poetry; 'Just the reverse' says the poetry is engaged in (held within) 'Rhymester engaged'.
explanation.definitionFit: Renga is a form of Japanese collaborative linked verse, the ancestor of haiku, composed by several poets in turn.

clue.text: Actor and playwright's plot with a monarch

parts.note: a plot is a scheme or plan
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the standard crossword queen

explanation.surface: A dramatist's storyline involves a king or queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' looks like a theatrical storyline to match the playwright, but it is a scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Planer, Neil in The Young Ones, is an English comic performer who has also written stage plays.

clue.text: A demon and I — we fight

definitions.note: the answer speaking as a body of warriors: a group that fights

parts.note: an imp is a little demon
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone and a devil declare themselves fighters.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the first person as the answer itself, a collective noun for warriors.
explanation.definitionFit: An impi is a regiment or armed band of Zulu warriors, so its members could say they are fighters.

clue.text: Ponderosa's one tree in part, not bay

indicators.note: not excludes something, so those letters are left out

parts.note: a branch is a part of a tree
B is the map abbreviation for bay

explanation.surface: A Ponderosa pine is a tree, but not a bay tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ponderosa' wants to be the pine tree, which suits 'tree' and 'bay'; it is the Cartwright family's spread in the US TV western Bonanza.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ponderosa was the Nevada cattle estate in Bonanza, an instance of a large farm for raising livestock.

clue.text: Poem I'd heard on champagne — very old and very dry

parts.note: Mumm is a French champagne house

indicators.note: something heard is taken by ear, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: If is Kipling's famous poem; said aloud with 'I'd' it gives the ending

explanation.surface: A poem recited over champagne, the wine described as aged and bone-dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very dry' sounds like wine-tasting language, matching the champagne, but it describes an embalmed body. 'On' puts the champagne first in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mummified body is ancient and preserved by drying out, so the word suits something both aged and parched.

clue.text: I can't locate North America when it's stormy

definitions.text: I can't locate North America when it's stormy

indicators.note: a storm tosses everything about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
NA is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A lost sailor in a gale complains that the far coast cannot be found.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue is the voice of a storm-tossed traveller from Europe, whose missing landfall lies across this water.
explanation.definitionFit: This ocean separates Europe from North America, so a voyager caught in its storms might fail to reach the far shore.
